title: The changed word
hook: his son Ram Rai alters a word of Nanak's hymn to please the court, and the Guru refuses to see him again

segments.voice: Yesterday, the herb garden, and a cure sent to the emperor's son. Your line was heal whoever asks. Did you help someone without keeping score? Day seventy-one.

You're in a meeting with the most powerful person you've ever met. They quote something your grandmother used to say, and ask what it means. The honest answer might annoy them. You can see it in their face. So you shade it. Just one word. Just enough to keep the room happy. It's so easy. It even has a polite name: being diplomatic. Now change two things. The thing you shaded wasn't your grandmother's saying. It was scripture. And the powerful person was the emperor. Today, the gentle seventh Guru draws the hardest line of his life, against his own son, over a single word.
screen: `THE MOST POWERFUL PERSON IN THE ROOM.` → `JUST ONE WORD, SHADED.` → `AND IT WAS SCRIPTURE.`

segments.voice: By 1661 there was a new emperor, Aurangzeb, who had fought his way to the throne, and he summoned Guru Har Rai to Delhi. The Guru didn't go himself. He sent his elder son, Ram Rai, a bright young man, to answer for the community. At court, tradition says, Ram Rai impressed everyone. Then came a hard question. Someone pointed to a line in Guru Nanak's writing, in the long hymn called Asa di Var. The line says, in plain words, that the clay of a Muslim's grave ends up in the potter's hands, kneaded into pots and bricks. It's a reflection on death: however a body is laid to rest, it becomes earth. The court heard it as an insult to Muslims. And Ram Rai, wanting to please, said it had been copied wrong. He changed the word Muslim to a word meaning a faithless person. It worked. The court was satisfied. When the news reached Kiratpur, the gentle Guru, the one who sent medicine even to the emperor's son, was unmoved. Tradition says he declared that Ram Rai had turned his back on the Guru's word, and he never saw his son again. He passed over him and chose his younger son, Har Krishan, as Guru. Why so hard, from so soft a man? Because for Sikhs, the Gurus' word is not anyone's to trade, not even a Guru's son's. In this story, gentleness with people and firmness about the word live in the same man: he would heal an emperor's son, but he would not let one word be edited to please a throne.
screen: `SUMMONED TO AURANGZEB'S COURT.` · `A LINE ABOUT CLAY AND THE POTTER.` · `RAM RAI CHANGES ONE WORD.` · `THE GURU NEVER SEES HIM AGAIN.` · then, large: `DON'T CHANGE THE WORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep one word you promised. Settle and breathe. Then bring to mind a promise you've made that's still open. To yourself, to a friend, to a child, to God if you pray. A small one is fine: I'll call. I'll come. I'll stop. Notice any way you've been quietly rewording it: I said I'd call, but a text counts. Just see it. Then let the original words stand, as they were said. The bell holds the time.
Ram Rai. Guru Har Rai's elder son, who altered one word of Guru Nanak's hymn to please the emperor's court, and whom his father never saw again.
Your line: don't change the word. Today, keep the promise you thought of, in the words you first said it. Day seventy-one.

howItsDone: Sikhs hold that the words of the Guru Granth Sahib must never be altered; the story of Ram Rai is told as the example of what happens when the word is changed to please power.

fork.setup: you're Ram Rai at the emperor's court. a line of Guru Nanak's has offended the room. what do you do?
options: explain what the line really means.
say it was copied wrong, and change one word.
fork.reveal: Ram Rai changed the word to please the court. it worked there, but his father never saw him again.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: Asa di Var, Guru Nanak's long hymn in raga Asa, traditionally sung in the early morning.

trapdoor: what you thought: a son said the wrong thing.
what it means: one word changed to please power, and a gentle Guru who drew his hardest line over it.
what a scholar hears: the line is in Asa di Var (Ang 466); Ram Rai later settled at Dehradun, and the city's name is often traced to his dera, his camp.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 466 (Asa di Var, slok of Guru Nanak on the clay of the grave and the potter)

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: hook no longer uses 'imagine' or 'everyone does it'; 'whatever we believe about burial or cremation' reworded so the narrator speaks for no one; the closing 'you don't edit what was given' instruction replaced with a description of the Guru; Dehradun etymology softened to 'often traced'; 'still sung each morning' softened.

The line 'mitti musalman ki pere pai kumhiar' (Ang 466) is paraphrased; Ram Rai's substitution of 'beiman' (faithless) for 'musalman' is tradition. Confirm Ang and paraphrase, and that the explanation of the line as a reflection on death is acceptable.
Date of the Delhi summons given as 1661; confirm.
Dehradun etymology (dera of Ram Rai) in the trapdoor: commonly stated; confirm.
The court's objection is framed as 'the court heard it as an insult to Muslims', neutrally; confirm tone toward Muslims and Islam.
Review edit: 'sent medicine to his enemies' changed to 'sent medicine even to the emperor's son' to match day 70 without overstating Dara Shikoh as the Guru's enemy.
